title: Fine-Tuning: LoRA, QLoRA & DPO
desc: Runnable code for adapter-based fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA) and the practical, production-favored alternative to classic RLHF: Direct Preference Optimization.
content:
Full fine-tuning a 7B+ model means updating every parameter — hundreds of gigabytes of optimizer state, multiple A100s, and a checkpoint you can't easily roll back. Almost nobody does this for domain adaptation anymore. Instead, production teams freeze the base model and train a tiny set of adapter weights on top. This chapter gives you exact, runnable code for the three techniques that matter: LoRA (adapter fine-tuning), QLoRA (adapter fine-tuning on a quantized base model, so it fits on one consumer GPU), and DPO (the preference-tuning step most teams now use instead of classic PPO-based RLHF).

🏷️
A note on "RLHF"
Classic RLHF trains a separate reward model, then optimizes the policy against it with PPO — two training loops, a lot of instability, and a lot of infrastructure. Almost no production team hand-rolls this anymore. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) reformulates the same objective as a single supervised loss over preference pairs, with no reward model and no RL loop. This chapter teaches DPO as the practical way to do RLHF-style alignment, and explains why it replaced PPO for most use cases.

LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation

A linear layer's weight matrix W (shape d × k) is frozen. LoRA adds a parallel path: two small matrices A (d × r) and B (r × k), where r (the rank) is typically 8–64 — orders of magnitude smaller than d or k. The effective weight becomes W + (alpha/r) · B·A. Only A and B are trained; W never moves.

Effective weight update
h = W₀x + ΔWx = W₀x + (α / r) · B(Ax)
LoRA freezes W₀ and trains only the low-rank pair (A, B). At r=16 on a 4096×4096 layer, that's ~131K trainable params vs 16.8M for the full matrix — a 128x reduction.
Python · LoRA supervised fine-tuning with peft + trl
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

model_id = "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto"
)

lora_config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,                    # adapter rank
    lora_alpha=32,            # scaling: alpha/r = 2.0
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    bias="none",
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"],
)
model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()  # ~0.6% of params trainable

# conversational dataset ("messages" column) — SFTTrainer applies the chat template automatically
dataset = load_dataset("HuggingFaceH4/no_robots", split="train")

training_args = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="./lora-out",
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    learning_rate=2e-4,
    num_train_epochs=3,
    max_length=1024,        # SFTConfig field — trl 0.12+ moved this off SFTTrainer's own kwargs
    bf16=True,
    logging_steps=10,
    save_strategy="epoch",
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=dataset,
)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("./lora-out/final-adapter")

QLoRA — LoRA on a Quantized Base

QLoRA changes exactly one thing: the frozen base model is loaded in 4-bit (NF4) instead of bf16/fp16. Gradients still flow through LoRA's A/B matrices in full precision — only the frozen weights are compressed. This is why a 7B model that needs ~14GB in bf16 fits in ~5GB in 4-bit, making LoRA fine-tuning possible on a single 24GB consumer GPU.

Python · QLoRA: 4-bit base + LoRA adapters
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, prepare_model_for_kbit_training

bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",           # normal-float 4-bit, best for weights
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, # matmuls upcast to bf16
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,      # quantize the quantization constants too
)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B",
    quantization_config=bnb_config,
    device_map="auto",
)
model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)  # casts norms to fp32, enables grad checkpointing

lora_config = LoraConfig(
    r=64, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0.1,
    bias="none", task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
                    "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
)
model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)
# ...same SFTConfig / SFTTrainer loop as the LoRA example above
💾
Why r=64 for QLoRA but r=16 above?
The original QLoRA paper found that with a quantized base, slightly higher rank (32–64) recovers quality lost to 4-bit quantization noise, at negligible extra memory cost since adapter matrices are tiny regardless. This is a starting point to tune, not a law.

Merging & Serving the Adapter

After training, you have two choices: merge the adapter into the base weights (single dense checkpoint, simplest to serve), or keep them separate and let the serving engine apply the adapter at load time (lets you swap adapters per-request).

Python · Merge adapter into base weights
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B", torch_dtype="bfloat16")
merged = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, "./lora-out/final-adapter")
merged = merged.merge_and_unload()  # folds B·A into W₀, returns a plain HF model
merged.save_pretrained("./merged-model")
🔀
Skip merging: serve adapters directly in vLLM
vLLM can load LoRA adapters at serve time without merging: vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B --enable-lora --lora-modules my-adapter=./lora-out/final-adapter. This lets one base-model deployment serve many fine-tuned variants, switching adapters per request via the model field — no duplicated GPU memory for the frozen weights.

DPO — Preference Tuning Without a Reward Model

Classic RLHF trains a reward model on human preference pairs, then runs PPO to maximize that reward — two training pipelines, KL penalties to keep the policy near the reference model, and notoriously unstable optimization. DPO shows the same optimal policy can be reached by directly optimizing a classification-style loss over preference pairs — no reward model, no RL loop, no sampling during training.

FieldMeaning
promptThe input the model sees
chosenThe response a human (or judge model) preferred
rejectedThe response that was dispreferred
Python · DPO fine-tuning on top of the SFT/LoRA checkpoint
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import PeftModel
from trl import DPOTrainer, DPOConfig

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("./merged-model")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("./merged-model", torch_dtype="bfloat16")

# Preference dataset: columns "prompt", "chosen", "rejected"
dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized", split="train")

config = DPOConfig(
    output_dir="./dpo-out",
    beta=0.1,                    # KL penalty strength vs reference policy
    per_device_train_batch_size=2,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=8,
    learning_rate=5e-6,        # DPO wants a MUCH lower LR than SFT
    num_train_epochs=1,
    bf16=True,
)

trainer = DPOTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=config,
    train_dataset=dataset,
    processing_class=tokenizer,   # builds its own frozen reference model internally
)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("./dpo-out/final")
⚠️
DPO learning rate is not SFT learning rate
DPO operates on log-probability ratios against a frozen reference model. Reusing an SFT-scale LR (1e-4 to 2e-4) will blow up the KL term and destroy the model's fluency within a few hundred steps. Start at 5e-6 to 1e-5 and watch the implicit reward margin, not just the loss.

PPO-Based RLHF vs DPO

Classic RLHF (reward model + PPO)
  • Two training stages: reward model, then PPO policy
  • PPO requires online sampling during training — slow, unstable
  • Needs a value/critic network and reward-hacking guardrails
  • State of the art through ~2023 (InstructGPT, GPT-4 alignment)
DPO
  • Single supervised-style loss over static preference pairs
  • No sampling loop, no reward model, no value network
  • More stable, far cheaper to run and debug
  • Now the default in most open and production alignment pipelines

Practical Gotchas

IssueGuidance
Catastrophic forgettingKeep LR low (1e-4–2e-4 for LoRA), mix in some general-purpose data alongside your task-specific set
Choosing rStart at 8–16 for narrow-domain SFT, 32–64 for QLoRA or broad instruction tuning
Choosing alphaA common heuristic is alpha = 2 × r; tune the ratio, not the absolute values, in isolation
Dataset sizeLoRA SFT can show gains from as few as 500–1,000 well-curated examples; DPO needs thousands of preference pairs to move the needle reliably
When full fine-tuning still winsLarge domain shifts (new language, new modality) where adapter capacity is the bottleneck, and you have the multi-GPU budget to justify it

🔑
Key Takeaways
1. LoRA trains a low-rank adapter pair instead of the full weight matrix — a 100x+ reduction in trainable parameters with comparable task performance. 2. QLoRA adds 4-bit quantization of the frozen base only, making fine-tuning fit on one consumer GPU. 3. Serve adapters unmerged via vLLM's LoRA support when you need to multiplex many fine-tunes over one base model. 4. DPO is the practical, stable replacement for PPO-based RLHF — same objective, one training loop, no reward model, and it needs a much lower learning rate than SFT.
